title: Can a Million AI Agents Create Superintelligence?
gist: Guest futurist Ramez Naam argues from benchmark data that parallel AI agents buy speed but show steeply sub-logarithmic gains in intelligence, so agent swarms are unlikely to make recursive self-improvement self-sustaining. He forecasts no sustained acceleration of Anthropic's progress through H1 2027.

insights.claim: Adding parallel AI agents buys much more speed than it buys higher problem-solving capability; multi-agent gains on harder problems diminish very quickly and may saturate.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Discount narratives that swarm size alone drives an AI intelligence explosion; watch per-task scaling data instead.
insights.quote: So far, using more agents buys us much more speed than extra capability.

insights.claim: Toby Ord's analysis of GPT-5.6 Sol finds four agents reach the same result 1.9x faster at about 2.1x token cost on Terminal-Bench, but 2.6x faster at about 1.6x cost on BrowseComp, because web research splits into independent searches while command-line tasks change a shared environment sequentially.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Parallelism pays where tasks decompose; token-spend economics for agents vary by workload.

insights.claim: On ProgramBench, Opus 5.5 with five agents gets about 2.7x its solo speed versus 2.2x for Opus 5, at lower cost, so newer Claude models are improving at the speed-cost tradeoff of parallel agents.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Model generations are getting more efficient at multi-agent execution, supporting agentic-workflow demand.

insights.claim: On Anthropic's Lean formal-math benchmark, the local speed exponent lambda falls from about 0.75 (10 to 30 agents) to about 0.33 (30 to 100 agents), so even speed gains taper as agent count rises.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Expect diminishing cost-efficiency when scaling agent counts into the hundreds.

insights.claim: Parallel agents are especially potent for offensive cybersecurity, where many targets or vulnerabilities can be tried at once without conceptual breakthroughs, though attacks on hardened targets requiring long attack chains may still saturate.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Cyber-risk from swarms is real even if swarm intelligence is overstated; relevant to security spending.

insights.claim: On SEC-Bench Pro, GPT-5.6 Sol scores about 71.2 with one agent, 74.3 with four and 76.4 with sixteen; each fourfold expansion adds fewer points (3.1 then 2.1), i.e. sub-logarithmic scaling.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that swarm gains flatten on a security task.

insights.claim: Noam Brown said he would not attribute even 10% of the credit for OpenAI's Navier-Stokes result (about 10,000 agents over 88 hours) to multi-agent, crediting the smarter underlying model.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Headline swarm results may really reflect model quality, so model capability is the key variable to track.
insights.quote: I wouldn’t even attribute 10% of the credit to multi-agent.

insights.claim: In Anthropic's Opus 5.5 Lean proof test on 49 theorem statements, the first tenfold agent increase adds 27 score points but the next tenfold adds only 2, even with a 100-agent team organized with twelve sub-leads, suggesting near-saturation.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Formal math proofs are the closest analog to conceptual breakthroughs, and they show steep plateauing.

insights.claim: Ten Opus 5.5 agents outscore a hundred Opus 5 or Fable 5.1 agents on formal math proofs, so a stronger base model does more than ten times the agents.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Capital is better spent on model quality than on swarm scale for hard problems.

insights.claim: Extrapolating Astra's test-time compute curve suggests it would need about 300 times the compute of OpenAI's internal model to match that model's lowest plotted score on curated math problems.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Test-time compute is a weak substitute for a better model.

insights.claim: A persona and model diversity study found substantial gains up to eight agents, after which average performance barely moved; the Artificial Hivemind study found strikingly similar open-ended outputs across models.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Homogeneous training data caps the value of copies; differentiated training is a research and investment angle.

insights.claim: Logarithmic scaling appears in Ryan Greenblatt's ARC program-sampling experiment and a 1-to-128-agent molecular exploration study, which is better than sub-log but still far weaker than RSI models assume.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Parallel search over verifiable spaces scales best; favors domains with cheap verification.

themes.theme: RSI models assume unrealistic parallel returns

insights.claim: Hypothetical software-RSI models assume strong returns to parallel labor: Chan et al. (2026) have doubling research labor raise software progress about 2.6x, and Davidson and Houlden use an exponent of 0.6 (0.3 if compute-bound); observed multi-agent curves look nothing like that.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Forecasts of an AI intelligence explosion rest on assumptions not yet matched by data; temper takeoff-driven trades.
insights.locator: What does this mean for runaway RSI

insights.claim: Power-law diminishing returns in machine learning have been observed for over thirty years (power-law learning curves measured in 1993), so breaking them would require a revolution, probably needing conceptual breakthroughs rather than more copies.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Base rate favors continued diminishing returns unless a new scaling axis emerges, as reasoning models did.
insights.locator: Intelligence gains face much harder diminishing returns

insights.claim: Naam's three conceptual limits on multi-agent scaling are coordination skill, homogeneity of thought, and problem structure (sequential dependencies).
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: A checklist for judging whether any agent-swarm claim will scale.

insights.claim: Earlier findings: OpenAI used 124x as many tokens per researcher but ran only 1.6x as many experiments, and the measured software feedback loop is roughly five to ten times too weak to be self-sustaining.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Compute spend per researcher is not translating one-for-one into research output.

insights.claim: Anthropic's October employment report shows research agents logging about nine hours per human work-hour by mid-July and nineteen by late August, which Naam treats as roughly fivefold then tenfold labor versus April.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: This is the live test of agent-driven research acceleration; watch Anthropic model release cadence.

insights.claim: Under different models, the labor increase implies April-to-August research pace of about 25x (Chan exponent), 2-4x (Davidson-Houlden), about 2x (log) or 1.1-1.8x (sub-log); with half of capability gains from software, a 4x software pace means only about 2.5x overall ECI slope.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Gives numeric thresholds to judge whether AI progress is accelerating in early 2027.

insights.claim: Naam predicts no sustained acceleration in Anthropic's AI progress as measured by ECI through the first half of 2027, likely at the low end of the sub-log scenarios, with a signal expected from about November-February 2027 after a six-month lag.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: If ECI jumps materially in early 2027, the skeptical view is wrong and AI-takeoff positioning deserves weight.
insights.quote: I don’t expect to see sustained acceleration of Anthropic’s AI progress

insights.claim: Naam proposes tracking G (score gain per team expansion), lambda (speed-cost exponent) and N (team size where gains saturate) across 1-10, 10-100 and 100-1000 agents for each new model.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: A dashboard of metrics to monitor whether swarm scaling is genuinely improving.
